senses: A falcon (Falco cherrug) native of Southern Europe and Asia.
A medium cannon slightly smaller than a culverin developed during the early 17th century.
ety: From Middle English sacre, from Middle French sacre, from Old Spanish sacro, from Arabic صَقْر (ṣaqr).

senses: The rank or jurisdiction of a viscount.
A smuggler of sheep or wool.
A pause or period of slackening.
examples: It rained without letup for many hours.
We waited for a letup in the rain, then we ran home before it started again.

senses: A cup-shaped mass at the base of various fungi.
The membranous covering which completely encloses many fungi in the early stage of growth.
examples: The genus Amanita has both a volva and a veil; the spores are white, and the stem is easily separable from the cap.

senses: Synonym of okra: the plant or its edible capsules.
ety: Borrowed from Hindi भिंडी (bhiṇḍī, “okra”), a feminine form of Sanskrit भिण्डा (bhiṇḍā).

senses: An electronic process that adds color to black and white movies.
Having a leaf, leaves or folds.
ety: From Middle English leuued, levyd, equivalent to leaf + -ed.

senses: A prokaryotic organism; a member of the domain Archaea
ety: Scientific Latin, corresponding to a singular form of Archaea.
examples: Then, the theory goes, a rogue archaeon gobbled up a bacterium to create an entirely new type of cell that would go on to form the basis of all complex life on Earth, from plants to humans.

senses: A perfume prepared from the flowers of Stephanotis floribunda.
A weight used in the 18th and 19th century in the Middle East and the East Indies, of no single standard but rather of varying sizes sometimes termed little bahars and great bahars.
ety: From Egyptian Arabic بهار (bahār) or other dialects, Arabic بُهَار (buhār).

senses: A long unpadded strap to pass over and keep in place a blanket, pack or saddle on an animal.
A piece of tack wrapped around the belly of a horse, to use when longeing.
A girdle to fasten a garment, especially a cassock.
ety: From Old French surcengle, formed with sur (“over”) and cengle (“girdle”).

senses: An elected village or neighborhood official in modern Turkey.
ety: From Turkish muhtar and Ottoman Turkish مختار (muhtar, “village headman”), from North Levantine Arabic مختار (“village headman”), from substantive application of Arabic مُخْتَار (muḵtār, “chosen”).

senses: The state of being in or reaching puberty.
A hood, or cape with a hood, made of or lined with grey fur, formerly worn by the clergy.
ety: From Middle English amit, from Old French emit, from Latin amictus, from amiciō (see there for more). Compare French amict, Italian amitto, Portuguese amicto.

senses: One who slanders or defames the name or reputation of another person.
The branch of biology dealing with reptiles (Reptilia) and amphibians (Amphibia).
ety: Derived from French herpétologie, from Ancient Greek ἑρπετόν (herpetón, “reptile”) + -logie (suffix indicating a field of study or work), equivalent to herpet- + -logy.

senses: Foretold or spoken of in advance.
To employ hydraulic fracturing (fracking).
ety: From an abbreviated form of fracture. Also found in English hydrofracking.

senses: A fashionable lady.
A sexual preference for adolescent girls.
Adult sexual attraction primarily towards pubescent children and younger adolescents, usually between 10 and 14 years old. Can fall under the same definition as pedophile.
examples: This finding, if confirmed, may offer a useful lead for research in heterosexual pedophilia or hebephilia (a preference for pubescent girls)

senses: Made of gold and ivory.
ety: From Ancient Greek χρυσελεφάντινος (khruselephántinos), from χρυσός (khrusós, “gold”) + ἐλεφάντινος (elephántinos, “of ivory”).

senses: A diacritic (゛) used with Japanese kana to mark a consonant as voiced.
ety: Borrowed from Japanese 点々(てんてん) (tenten, literally “dots”).

senses: Any of several waterbirds in the family Podicipedidae of the order Podicipediformes. They have strong, sharp bills, and lobate toes.
Synonym of goldish.
ety: From Middle English goldy, equivalent to gold + -y.

senses: One who values precision.
An artist working in the style of precisionism.
A great success; a hit.
ety: Entertainment industry slang; possibly from box office or buffo.

senses: Sweepings; refuse.
ety: From Old French rif et raf (“one and all”), of Germanic origin. The first word is from rifler (“to scrape off”) and the last is from raffler, related to rafler (“to plunder”).

senses: A student of, or expert in, penology.
The formation of a solid by cooling; freezing.
The formation of a gel, especially from a sol.
ety: From Latin gelātiō (“freezing”), from gelātus (“frozen”), past participle of gelō (“to freeze”).

senses: A fortified tower built in biblical times.
examples: The building has been called a “migdal” (Hebrew “fortress”) temple because of its massive walls, up to fifteen feet thick; its two towers at the entrance; and its presumed second or even third stories.
Migdals or towers, part of temple precincts, were places of refuge.

senses: Characterized by shouting; prone to shouting.
Harsh and strident.
examples: In A League of Their Own (1992), as the shouty baseball coach to an all-girls team, he's once again a curmudgeonly but lovable mentor figure.
That is the key - understanding the issues and saying things that accurately reflect the passengers' insight, rather than being just another of the shouty voices from the sidelines.

senses: A vehicle or other object having a specified tonnage, or weighing a specified number of tons.
The nest of a bird of prey.
Any high and remote but commanding place.
ety: From Middle English eire, aire, from Old French aire or Medieval Latin aeria. Old French aire, in the sense of an eagle's nest, may have derived from Latin ager, or may less likely be related to the other senses, ultimately from Latin ārea.

senses: A gunfight; a battle involving gunfire
The underlying science of nanotechnology.
A crossbreed of a poodle and another breed of dog.
ety: From the -oodle ending of mixed breed names such as Labradoodle.
examples: For quotations using this term, see Citations:oodle.

senses: Not gentlemanly; not adhering to the high moral standards expected of a gentleman; impolite, unchivalrous, or indecent.
examples: My grandmother thought it was ungentlemanly of my boyfriend to suggest that we split the bill for dinner.

senses: A Filipino sword akin to the kris.
ety: Borrowed from Tagalog kalis, from Malay keris, from Old Javanese kĕris, kris Doublet of kris.

senses: The brahmin varna in Hinduism. (Plural: brahmana.)
A brahmin; a member of the brahmana (sense 1).
A prose text that explains aspects of the Vedas.
